definition.text: A proposed global framework that shrinks total greenhouse gas emissions to a safe level while bringing every country's emissions per person to the same level.

facts.text: It was conceived by the Global Commons Institute in the early 1990s and is expressed as a simple mathematical formula.
Emission entitlements start from current emissions and move toward equal shares per person at a negotiated rate of convergence.
Earlier convergence gives more entitlements to low-emitting, typically poorer, countries; the rate is described as a key equity lever.
Critics say a per-person basis could reward population growth, so the model lets negotiators fix a population base year.

definition.text: Pressuring institutions to sell off stocks, bonds and other investments in fossil fuel extraction companies, as a way to fight climate change.

facts.text: It began on US university campuses in 2011, and by 2015 was reportedly the fastest-growing divestment movement in history.
As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions with over $40.5 trillion in assets had begun or committed to some form of divestment.
Divesters act to align investments with values, to fight the fossil fuel industry, or to protect portfolios from climate-related financial risk.
One financial motive is stranded assets, the 'carbon bubble': reserves that cannot be burned safely and would have to be written off.
Its aim is to speed the renewable energy transition by stigmatising fossil fuel companies.
Fossil fuel companies have partly blamed divestment pressure for their rising cost of capital.

definition.text: The agreement reached at the 2021 UN climate conference (COP26) in Glasgow.

facts.text: It was the first climate agreement explicitly planning to reduce unabated coal use.
A pledge to 'phase out' coal was changed late in the talks to 'phase down', at the urging of coal-reliant countries such as India and China.
Countries agreed to revisit their emission plans in 2022 to keep the 1.5 °C target within reach, and committed to climate finance for developing countries.
Around it, more than 140 countries had pledged net-zero emissions and more than 100 pledged to reverse deforestation by 2030.

title: Global climate regime

definition.text: The worldwide framework of rules for regulating how human activity affects the climate system, in order to limit climate change.

facts.text: Its framework was set by the UNFCCC, and its first legally binding result was the Kyoto Protocol.
Between 2013 and 2015 there was no legally binding global climate regime, and the voluntary Copenhagen Accord pledges served in practice.
The 2015 Paris Agreement became the regime, with all countries signed on to balancing greenhouse gas sources and sinks in the second half of the century.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
